specPoints.text: understand the reasons for pest control and the advantages and disadvantages of using pesticides and biological control with crop plants

primer.text: Pests compete with farmers for every harvest, and two very different toolkits answer them. Chemical pesticides strike fast but carry resistance and collateral damage; biological control enlists living predators that persist for seasons. This note weighs both sets of advantages and disadvantages.

lessons.title: Chemical Control: Fast, Cheap, Blunt
sourceHeadings: Using pest control to increase crop yields
lessons.opening: Insects chew leaves, weeds steal water and nutrients, and fungi spread disease through a crop, so farmers reach for pesticides to cut the losses. Chemical control acts immediately and kills whole pest populations, but resistance, harm to useful species and build-up in food chains are the price.
keyPoints: Pesticides reduce crop damage by killing the insects, weeds and fungi that compete with or attack the crop.
Insecticide products kill insect pests, herbicide products kill weeds, and fungicides kill fungal pests.
Chemical control is cheap to buy, works at once, and can wipe out the entire pest population present.
Pests can evolve resistance to a chemical, forcing repeated reapplication.
Non-specific chemicals may kill beneficial organisms such as pollinating bees.
Persistent chemicals resist breakdown and can undergo bioaccumulation, damaging predators high up in food chains.

low.restatement: Spray kills the pests today — cheap and total — but pests adapt, helpful bugs die, and the chemical climbs food chains.
low.analogy: A sledgehammer: one swing flattens the problem and half the furniture.
low.examPointer: Name bioaccumulation when explaining harm to top predators — the term itself is on the mark scheme.

medium.restatement: Chemical control with insecticides, herbicides and fungicides delivers immediate, population-wide reductions in crop competitors, yet pests evolve resistance, beneficial species such as bees are killed alongside targets, persistent compounds accumulate up food chains, and sprays must be reapplied season after season.
medium.analogy: Paying a debt instantly with a loan that keeps charging interest — the pest problem eases today while resistance and residue costs accrue.
medium.examPointer: Balance answers as advantage-then-disadvantage pairs; examiners reward the contrast, not just the list.

check.stem: Which pesticide family targets unwanted plants growing among a crop?

options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Insecticides target insect pests.
Fungicides target fungal infections.
Bacteria are not the weeding target.

check.stem: What immediate benefit do pesticides give a farmer?

options.text: A rapid reduction in pest numbers protecting the current crop
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.

options.text: A permanent end to all pest problems
options.explanation: Resistance and reapplication contradict that.

options.text: Fertilisation of the soil as a side effect
options.explanation: Pesticides kill pests; they do not feed the crop.

options.text: Better flavour in the harvested produce
options.explanation: Flavour is not the mechanism.

check.stem: Why can insecticide use damage a crop's pollination?

options.text: Non-specific chemicals may kill bees and other pollinators visiting the crop
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Bees avoid any field with crops
options.explanation: Bees visit crops actively.
Sterility is not the taught mechanism.
Repulsion is not how non-specific toxicity works.

check.stem: What does bioaccumulation threaten in an ecosystem?

options.text: Predators near the top of food chains gather harmful chemical concentrations
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.
Persistence harms predators, not fertility.
Residues do not feed the crop.
Resistance is an evolution outcome, not bioaccumulation.

check.stem: A farm has used the same insecticide for a decade and it now fails. What happened?

options.text: The pest population evolved resistance to the chemical
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Expiry dates are not the taught cause.
The crop is unchanged; the pest adapted.
Washing is loss, not failure of action.

check.stem: State two advantages of using chemical pesticides on crops.
check.modelAnswer: They act immediately and they are relatively cheap and accessible, killing the whole pest population present.

check.stem: Name the three pesticide types matched to insects, weeds and fungi.
check.modelAnswer: Insecticides kill insects, herbicides kill weeds, and fungicides kill fungal pests.

check.stem: Explain why pesticides usually need to be applied repeatedly across a season.
check.modelAnswer: New pests arrive or hatch after each application, and surviving resistant individuals breed, so one treatment never clears the population for long.

check.stem: An orchard borders a beekeeper's hives. Recommend a control choice and justify it.
check.modelAnswer: Avoid broad-spectrum insecticide sprays during flowering because non-specific chemicals would kill the pollinating bees, and choose a targeted or biological approach instead.

lessons.title: Biological Control: Predators on Payroll
lessons.opening: Biological control hires the pest's natural enemies. Parasitic wasps patrol glasshouse tomatoes against whitefly, and ladybirds snack on aphids outdoors. Because the method rides a predator-prey cycle it never wipes the pest out, but it lasts, targets narrowly and skips chemical pollution.
keyPoints: A natural predator species is introduced deliberately to prey on the pest.
Classic pairings include parasitic wasps controlling whitefly in glasshouse tomatoes and ladybirds eating aphids.
The predator-prey cycle holds the pest at low levels rather than eliminating it completely.
Advantages: specific targeting, no chemical pollution, no resistance evolving, long-lasting effect without repeated application.
Disadvantages: the predator may eat other organisms, needs time to work, never removes every pest, may fail to settle or even become a pest itself.

low.restatement: Put something that eats the pest into the field; it stays for seasons, never finishes the job, but no chemicals needed.
low.analogy: Hiring a cat for the barn — patient, self-sufficient, and it never catches every mouse.
low.examPointer: When comparing methods, quote the predator-prey cycle wording: control, not eradication.

medium.restatement: Biological control introduces a predator chosen to attack the pest, so populations settle into a cycle that suppresses but never eradicates the pest; the method is specific and durable without pollution or resistance, but it acts slowly, may attack other species, and the introduced predator might struggle or turn troublesome.
medium.analogy: A security guard stationed on site: vigilant for months, unlikely to chase every intruder, and occasionally guilty of misidentifying a guest.
medium.examPointer: Give the whitefly-wasp glasshouse example — concrete cases convert explanation marks into fact marks.

check.stem: What does biological control use to suppress a pest species?

options.text: A natural predator or parasite introduced against it
options.explanation: Correct — this follows directly from the definition.
Chemicals define the other method.
Crop modification is not this technique.
Barriers are exclusion, not biological control.

check.stem: Which pairing is a standard example of biological control in glasshouses?

options.text: Parasitic wasps hunting whitefly on tomatoes
options.explanation: Yes — the mechanism works exactly this way.
Ladybirds prey on aphids; they are not pollinators here.
Bees pollinate; they do not hunt fungus.
Netting is physical exclusion.

check.stem: Why does biological control leave some pests alive in the crop?

options.text: The predator-prey cycle stabilises the pest at low numbers instead of erasing it
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.

options.text: Predators refuse to hunt to completion
options.explanation: Cycle dynamics, not fussiness, keep prey present.
Hiding is not the mechanism described.
Established predators persist for long periods.

check.stem: Which disadvantage of biological control involves the introduced species itself?

options.text: It may fail to establish in the new area, or even become a pest
options.explanation: Right — this is the account the lesson teaches.

options.text: It always mutates into a super-predator
options.explanation: Mutation claims are not part of the account.
Pollution is a chemical-control drawback.
Resistance concerns chemicals, not predators.

check.stem: A grower needs pest suppression that lasts several seasons without respraying. Which method fits?

options.text: Biological control, because its effect is long-lasting
options.explanation: Right — the other options each misplace a concept.
Chemicals need repeated application.
Herbicides target weeds, and still need reapplication.
Glass is structural, not pest control.

check.stem: State two advantages of biological control over chemical pesticides.
check.modelAnswer: It causes no chemical pollution and the pest does not develop resistance, with effects lasting a long time.

check.stem: Give the classic outdoor example of one insect eating another.
check.modelAnswer: Ladybirds eat aphids, a natural predator-prey pairing used in biological control.

check.stem: Explain why biological control can target a pest species specifically.
check.modelAnswer: The introduced predator is chosen because it naturally attacks that pest, so the suppression falls on one species while most others go untouched.

check.stem: Whitefly numbers rise in a tomato glasshouse. Outline the biological response and one monitoring step.
check.modelAnswer: Introduce parasitic wasps to prey on the whitefly, then monitor leaves weekly to confirm the pest stays at low levels without chemical sprays.

glossary.definition: A chemical applied to kill unwanted organisms that damage crops.
Using a natural predator or parasite to suppress a pest species.
The build-up of a persistent chemical along a food chain, harming top predators.
The evolved ability of a pest population to survive a chemical that once killed it.
